vignette:
For Amar, the world split into before and after on a Tuesday evening in late October. They had been cycling home from their office in the city, a route they had taken for years, when a patrol car pulled them over for what the officer later claimed was a rolling stop at a deserted intersection. What Amar remembers is not the stop itself, but the feeling of being pulled off their bicycle, the asphalt scraping their palms, the weight of a knee pressed into their lower back while a voice shouted commands that seemed to come from very far away. They remember thinking, with absurd clarity, I am going to die on this street-and then nothing. The next thing they knew, they were sitting on a curb, a different officer offering them a bottle of water, their bicycle lying twisted on the grass. They have never been able to tell the story in sequence. When they try to reconstruct it, the middle dissolves into a smear of sensation: the cold ground, the pressure, the smell of someone's coffee-scented breath. The parts they cannot bear to reach-the moment the knee pressed down, the sound of their own voice pleading-they push away before the memory can fully form. Sometimes, without warning, the full weight of that terror crashes over them while they are sitting at their desk, or lying in bed, or, most confusingly, when they feel a moment of genuine happiness or relaxation. A wave of dread will rise from nowhere, leaving them breathless and confused, with no image attached to it.

In the months that followed, Amar's life contracted around invisible boundaries. At work, they now scan every meeting room before choosing a seat, always positioning themselves with their back to a wall and a clear line of sight to the door. Their colleagues have noticed that they flinch when someone enters a room abruptly, and they have stopped attending the weekly team stand-ups in the open-plan area because the unpredictable movement of people behind them feels unbearable. The worst moments come during their commute. They cannot see a person on a bicycle without their chest tightening, their palms sweating, a surge of adrenaline that makes them want to bolt. They have stopped cycling entirely, though it was their primary form of exercise and transport. Their spouse, Priya, has taken over the school run for their children, and Amar has begun working from home three days a week, citing a vague "back problem" to their manager.

Confrontations have become unmanageable. A disagreement with a colleague about a code review sent Amar into a spiral of hypervigilance that lasted three days-they watched the colleague's every gesture for signs of threat, replayed the conversation obsessively, and ultimately submitted a leave request. They have come to believe that danger is invisible, that anyone at any moment could turn into a source of harm. The old belief that the world was predictable, that people were generally good, that safety was something you could assume-all of that is gone. What remains is a constant, exhausting vigilance. Amar watches strangers on the street, in the grocery store, in the elevator of their own building, cataloguing potential threats. They are certain that others can see what happened to them, that the trauma is written on their face, visible to anyone who looks closely enough.

What finally brought Amar to seek help was a moment that should have been ordinary. Their daughter asked them to teach her to ride a bicycle. Amar stood in the driveway, unable to move, and said no. Priya watched them, and Amar saw in her eyes something they had been dreading: a recognition that something was deeply wrong. They are afraid of what therapy might uncover-afraid that if they let themselves remember fully, they will not be able to put the pieces back together. But they are more afraid of the life they are already living: a life of seats chosen for escape routes, of avoided streets and cancelled plans, of a bicycle rusting in the garage. They do not know if they can ever feel safe again. They only know that they cannot go on like this.
